sections.Overview:
Patellofemoral pain (PFP) is pain around or behind the patella, aggravated by at least one weight-bearing activity that loads the patellofemoral joint (PFJ) on a flexed knee — squatting, stair ambulation, running, hopping or jumping (2016 Manchester consensus).

Supporting but non-essential features: crepitus, patellar facet tenderness, small effusion, and pain on prolonged sitting or on rising from sitting.

Exclusion: a history of patellar dislocation or subluxation places the patient outside the PFP definition — that is patellar instability, a separate presentation.

Terminology to avoid: "patellofemoral pain syndrome" is discouraged by consensus. "Chondromalacia patellae" is an imaging or arthroscopic cartilage finding, not a synonym. "Maltracking" describes a mechanism, not a diagnosis.

Three-point summary

  • A clinical diagnosis of pattern plus exclusion — there is no definitive confirmatory test.
  • Combined hip and knee exercise is the best-supported intervention; wait-and-see is the worst option.
  • It is not self-limiting: 57% report unfavourable recovery at 5–8 years.
sections.Epidemiology & risk factors:
Prevalence and incidence

  • Adolescents: prevalence 7–28%, incidence 9.2% (2016 consensus).
  • Approximately 1 in 14 adolescents and up to 1 in 5 adults in selected populations at any one time (IASP).
  • Military recruits: annual incidence 3.8% (men) and 6.5% (women); prevalence 12% (men) and 15% (women).
  • Most common in physically active populations — runners, military recruits, jumping and court athletes.

Risk factors

Single-sport specialisationRR 1.5 (95% CI 1.0–2.2) vs multisport athletes

Muscle strengthConflicting evidence as a prospective risk factor
BMI or body fat %Not a risk factor (moderate–strong evidence)

Note the direction of travel: several factors long taught as causal have been excluded prospectively. Aetiology is considered multifactorial and remains poorly understood.
sections.Pathoanatomy & mechanism:
Structures involved. Articular cartilage is aneural and cannot itself be the pain source. Candidate nociceptive tissues are the richly innervated subchondral bone, infrapatellar fat pad, retinaculum, synovium and peripatellar soft tissue.

Working mechanism. Elevated or poorly distributed PFJ stress, where stress = joint reaction force ÷ contact area. PFJ reaction force rises steeply with knee flexion angle under load, which is why squatting, stairs and prolonged sitting provoke symptoms.

The common thread is load exceeding tissue capacity — a change in training volume, intensity, surface or footwear, or a return to activity after a break.

What has weakened. The structural "maltracking" model is no longer sufficient on its own. Imaging findings correlate poorly with symptoms, and many asymptomatic people show the same features.

Psychosocial contribution. Psychological factors are associated with symptom severity and predict clinical outcome. A biopsychosocial framing is now recommended rather than a purely mechanical one.
sections.Clinical presentation:
Area and nature. Diffuse, dull, aching retropatellar or peripatellar pain that the patient struggles to localise — often indicated with a whole-hand grasp over the kneecap rather than a fingertip. Frequently bilateral.

Aggravating factors (at least one weight-bearing, loaded-flexion activity is required for the diagnosis):

  • Squatting and deep knee flexion
  • Stair ambulation — descent is typically worse than ascent
  • Running, particularly downhill
  • Hopping and jumping
  • Prolonged sitting with the knee flexed, and rising from sitting (the "theatre sign")

Easing factors. Rest, extension, reduced loaded flexion.

24-hour pattern. Typically activity-dependent rather than a morning or night pattern. Constant or night pain is not typical of PFP and should prompt screening for bone stress injury, infection or malignancy.

Onset. Usually insidious, often traceable to a change in training load. An acute traumatic onset points elsewhere.

Other features. Crepitus, a small effusion, and a sense of the knee "giving way" — which is pain inhibition or quadriceps avoidance, not true mechanical instability.

Irritability (SIN). Usually low to moderate: pain comes on at a reasonably predictable point in the aggravating activity and settles within minutes to hours of stopping. High irritability or rapidly escalating pain warrants reconsidering the diagnosis.

Red flags for this presentation

  • Any adolescent with knee pain — examine the hip. Missing a SUFE is the single highest-consequence error in this presentation.
  • Constant, unremitting or night pain
  • Fever, systemic illness, hot swollen joint
  • Focal bony tenderness with a load-change or low-energy-availability history
  • True locking or a large or rapidly recurring effusion
  • Unexplained weight loss, a history of malignancy, or a palpable mass
sections.Subjective examination:
QuestionWhat it tells youShifts probability toward
"Point to where it hurts with one finger."Diffuse whole-hand grasp vs a single pointDiffuse → PFP; inferior pole point → patellar tendinopathy

Patient goals and expectations. Record the specific activity the patient wants back and the timeframe they expect. Expectation of recovery is itself prognostic.

Psychosocial screen. Screen for kinesiophobia, catastrophising and low self-efficacy — these are associated with severity and predict outcome. Consider the TSK, PCS or PSEQ where indicated.

Pain intensity is prognostic — record it. Usual pain >35/100 and worst pain >60/100 on VAS predicted unfavourable outcome at 12 months (Collins et al. 2013).
sections.Objective examination:
The key point: the 2016 consensus states plainly that "there is no definitive clinical test to diagnose PFP." The diagnosis is made on the symptom pattern with alternatives excluded.

Observation. Standing alignment, quadriceps bulk and VMO appearance, swelling, foot posture. Treat observed "maltracking" as a hypothesis, not a finding.

Range of motion. Usually full. The 2016 consensus notes ROM and effusion have limited diagnostic usefulness for PFP.

Strength testing. Quadriceps, hip abductors and hip external rotators — for treatment planning and baseline measurement, not for diagnosis. Hand-held dynamometry where available; otherwise single-leg heel raise, single-leg sit-to-stand and a timed side plank.

Functional tests. Double-leg squat, single-leg squat, step-down, and the activity the patient reports as aggravating. Reproduction of the concordant pain is the finding that matters.

Neurological screen and adjacent joints. Clear the hip and lumbar spine in every patient, and always in an adolescent.

TestAccuracySource
Pain during squatting — best available testPFP present in ~80% of those who test positive2016 Manchester consensus Part 1
Patellar edge / facet tendernessPFP present in 71–75% of those with this finding (limited evidence)2016 Manchester consensus Part 1
Patellar grind (Clarke's test)Low sensitivity, limited diagnostic accuracy — not recommended2016 Manchester consensus Part 1
Patellar apprehensionLimited accuracy for PFP; useful for instability2016 Manchester consensus Part 1
Knee ROM and effusionLimited diagnostic usefulness2016 Manchester consensus Part 1

Sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios are not reported for these tests in the consensus statement — the figures above are proportions of positives with PFP, which is not the same as a likelihood ratio. Do not convert them into LRs.
sections.Imaging & investigations:
Imaging is not routinely indicated. PFP is a clinical diagnosis, and PFJ imaging findings correlate poorly with symptoms.

When to image

  • Red flags — suspected bone stress injury, infection, malignancy
  • Acute trauma meeting the Ottawa knee rules
  • True mechanical locking or recurrent effusion — consider osteochondral or meniscal lesion
  • Failure to respond to an adequate trial of well-executed, progressively loaded exercise
  • Adolescent with knee or hip pain and restricted hip internal rotation — urgent pelvic imaging for SUFE

Preferred modality. Weight-bearing plain radiographs (including a skyline view) if PFJ OA or a bony lesion is suspected; MRI for suspected bone stress injury or osteochondral lesion.

When to refer on. Red flags, diagnostic uncertainty after thorough assessment, or suspected instability requiring surgical opinion.

What consensus recommends. The 2016 statement recommends a standard core set covering pain, function and global assessment, with quality of life and physical activity as optional constructs. It notes that few PROMs were developed specifically for PFP, so commonly used instruments may lack content validity.

Prognostically useful threshold: an AKPS score below 70/100 predicted unfavourable outcome at 5–8 years (Lankhorst et al. 2015). Record it at baseline.
sections.Management:
What the 2018 consensus supports (5th International Patellofemoral Pain Research Retreat, Gold Coast):

Dosage. The consensus explicitly states that the optimal exercise dose is unknown and that exercise prescription is poorly reported in the literature. The parameters below are therefore extrapolated from general strength-training principles, not from PFP-specific evidence. [verify]

Phase 1 · Settle and educate

Goals: reduce pain to a tolerable level, establish understanding, modify provocative load without full rest.

Interventions: education (mandatory at the first consultation), relative load modification, isometric quadriceps work, hip abductor and external rotator activation, prefabricated orthoses if foot-related aggravation.

Dosage [verify]: isometrics 5 × 45 s at ~70% MVC, 1–2× daily; pain during exercise acceptable up to 2–3/10 and settling within 24 h.

Progress when: pain predictable and settling within 24 h; able to perform a pain-acceptable squat to 60°.

Phase 2 · Load

Goals: build hip and knee strength and PFJ load tolerance.

Interventions: combined hip and knee strengthening — the single best-supported element. Squat and leg press through a tolerable range, split squats, step-ups and step-downs, hip abduction and external rotation under load.

Dosage [verify]: 3–4 sets × 8–12 reps at RPE 7–8, 2–3×/week, progressed weekly by load rather than reps.

Progress when: strength symmetry approaching the uninvolved side, pain-free through full functional range, AKPS improving.

Phase 3 · Return to load

Goals: restore the specific activity the patient wants back.

Interventions: graded reintroduction of the provocative activity, plyometrics and running progression where relevant, continued strength maintenance.

Dosage [verify]: graded exposure with 24-hour symptom response as the progression gate; strength maintained at 2×/week.

Progress when: target activity tolerated at full volume with stable 24-hour response.
sections.Education & self-management:
Education is the minimum intervention. Consensus is that at minimum, patients should receive education at the first consultation, and that a wait-and-see approach is the least effective option for short-term outcomes and should be avoided.

Key messages

  • This is a load problem, not a damaged joint. Cartilage is not being "worn away" by exercise.
  • Pain during rehabilitation is acceptable within limits and does not signal harm.
  • Rest alone makes it worse — capacity falls while demand stays the same.
  • Improvement takes months, not weeks. Set that expectation at the first visit.
  • Adherence to the strength program is the main determinant of outcome.

Load and activity advice. Modify rather than cease: reduce depth of knee flexion under load, reduce running volume or hills, spread sitting with periodic extension. Keep the patient active in a tolerable form.

Shared decision-making. The IASP fact sheet notes no single exercise or orthosis is superior, so patient preference, time and cost can legitimately guide the choice between options.
sections.Medical & surgical management:
There is no established surgical role in uncomplicated PFP. Surgery is relevant to patellar instability, osteochondral lesions and advanced PFJ osteoarthritis — all of which are different diagnoses.

When to refer

  • Red flags — suspected infection, malignancy, bone stress injury, SUFE
  • Recurrent patellar dislocation or demonstrable instability
  • Mechanical locking or a persistent effusion
  • Failure to progress after an adequate, well-executed and progressively loaded exercise program

Medical options. Simple analgesia or a short NSAID course may assist participation in rehabilitation but is not a treatment for the condition. Corticosteroid injection has no established role.
sections.Prognosis:
PFP is not self-limiting. This is the most commonly misunderstood aspect of the condition, and it should change how you counsel the patient.

TimepointOutcomeSource
12 months40% report unfavourable recovery despite evidence-based physiotherapyCollins et al. 2013
5–8 years57% report unfavourable recoveryLankhorst et al. 2015
Adolescents, 2 yearsUp to 65% still have painIASP fact sheet
Adolescents, 5 yearsUp to 40% still have painIASP fact sheet
Adolescents, 1–20 years50–90% report persistent symptomsRathleff et al.; Nimon et al.; Stathopulu & Baildam

Predictors of worse outcome

  • Symptom duration greater than 12 months (at 5–8 years) — Lankhorst et al. 2015
  • AKPS below 70/100 (at 5–8 years) — Lankhorst et al. 2015
  • Usual or resting pain above 35/100 VAS (at 12 months) — Collins et al. 2013
  • Worst or activity-related pain above 60/100 VAS (at 12 months) — Collins et al. 2013

Clinical implication. Symptom duration is the one prognostic factor you can influence by acting early. Prompt, relevant treatment at first presentation may improve long-term outcome — which is the strongest argument against wait-and-see.
sections.Return to sport or work:
Criteria, not time. There is no PFP-specific validated return-to-sport battery. Progress on symptom response and capacity.

Suggested criteria [verify]

  • Pain ≤2/10 during the target activity, settling within 24 hours
  • Quadriceps and hip abductor strength symmetry within 10–15% of the uninvolved limb
  • Pain-acceptable single-leg squat and step-down to the required depth
  • Where jumping or running is required: symmetrical hop performance and tolerance of a graded plyometric progression
  • AKPS improved by at least the MCID from baseline

Graded return. Reintroduce the provocative component last — depth of squat, hill running, jump volume — and use the 24-hour symptom response as the gate for each step up.

Work. For kneeling, squatting or stair-heavy occupations, stage the return by cumulative time in loaded flexion rather than by total hours.
sections.Clinical pearls & exam traps:
Clinical pearls

  • Ask the patient to point with one finger. A whole-hand grasp over the patella supports PFP; a fingertip on the inferior pole points to patellar tendinopathy.
  • Squatting pain is the best available test — present in roughly 80% of those who test positive.
  • Prefabricated orthoses are supported; custom orthoses are not. This catches people out in both directions.
  • Tell the patient at visit one that this takes months. Unmet expectation drives disengagement and disengagement drives the 57% figure.

Common exam traps

  • Clarke's test / patellar grind. Low sensitivity, limited accuracy, and unpleasant for the patient. Naming it as your diagnostic test is a mark lost.
  • Any adolescent with knee pain. If you do not examine the hip, you have failed the station — SUFE and Perthes both present as knee pain.
  • Calling it "chondromalacia" or "maltracking." Neither is a synonym for PFP.
  • Recommending rest. Wait-and-see is the least effective option for short-term outcome.
  • Treating a patient with a dislocation history as PFP. That is patellar instability by definition.
  • Knee-only strengthening. Consensus prefers combined hip and knee.

Viva questions

  • "Which single clinical test confirms PFP?" — None. State that, then describe the pattern-plus-exclusion approach.
  • "Why not just rest it?" — Capacity falls, demand is unchanged; wait-and-see performs worst short term.
  • "A 13-year-old with anterior knee pain — what must you not miss?" — SUFE and Perthes. Examine the hip.
  • "What would you tell this patient about their prognosis?" — Honest framing: ~40% unfavourable at 1 year, 57% at 5–8 years; early treatment and adherence are the levers.
sections.Evidence summary:
Clinical practice guidance. Two international consensus statements from the Patellofemoral Pain Research Retreats (2016 Manchester, 2018 Gold Coast) are the primary sources, supplemented by the JOSPT clinical practice guideline and the IASP fact sheet.

SourceDesignNHMRC levelKey finding
2016 Manchester consensus, Part 1International consensus statementExpert consensusDefines PFP; no definitive clinical test; squat pain is the best available
2018 Gold Coast consensusInternational consensus statementExpert consensusExercise therapy appropriate; combined hip and knee preferred; electrophysical agents and isolated mobilisation inappropriate
Lankhorst et al. 2015Multicentre observational cohortIII-257% unfavourable at 5–8 years; duration >12 months and AKPS <70 predict worse outcome
Collins et al. 2013Multicentre observational cohortIII-240% unfavourable at 12 months; baseline pain intensity predicts outcome
Hip and knee strengthening meta-analysis (JOSPT 2018)Systematic review with meta-analysisIHip and knee strengthening more effective than knee alone for pain and activity

Evidence quality. Intervention evidence is moderate and consistent for exercise. Diagnostic evidence is weak — no test has adequate accuracy. Aetiological evidence is weak and several long-assumed risk factors have been prospectively excluded.
